newsitem.title: USA: IBM employee buyout plan expected Thursday.
newsitem.headline: IBM employee buyout plan expected Thursday.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. is expected to announce a voluntary buyout plan to its eligible employees Thursday, sources said.
A spokesman for the Armonk, N.Y.-based computer giant declined to comment, but the sources said the company intends to rebalance its work force and redeploy its resources.
The buyout plan is likely to be aimed at U.S. employees in non-strategic and support functions at many U.S. locations. IBM is not expected to disclose the number of staff targeted.
But analysts said the move is aimed at getting 6,000 to 10,000 employees worldwide out of its slower growth areas.
"The goal is to get as many people as possible to take it," said one industry source who asked not to be identified.
Layoffs could result if an insufficient number of employees accept the offer, analysts said.

Employees also may be offered jobs at IBM's faster-growing units, such as its services business, which has added about 10,000 jobs this year and plans to add 4,000 to 5,000 more before the end of the year.
IBM had a total worldwide work force of 225,000, with 110,000 of those employees in the United States, at the end of 1995.

While sources said IBM is only targeting the U.S. "infrastructure" staff with the buyout plan, analysts said they believe there are several slower growth areas of its business where IBM could trim its staff, such as maintenance, certain mainframe manufacturing, storage and some European areas where it is difficult to lay off workers.
"You just look at the mainframe business," said John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst.

"Look at how efficient it is to manufacture (the newer) CMOS mainframes vs. the water-cooled bipolar models," Jones added. "You don't need the personnel to manufacture those products anymore. There is a natural reduction in head count."

The buyout plan will likely entail one week of pay for every six months of employment at IBM with a ceiling of six months pay, analysts speculated. Only certain employees, such as those having employement over five years, are eligible.
Analysts do not expect a charge for the buyout plan because IBM has told analysts to include $800 million for restructuring costs into their financial models this year.

But if not enough employees take the plan, layoffs are very possible before the end of the year, analysts and sources said. As one possible inducement for employees, IBM considered raising its age for full retirement benefits from the current 55 to 60 or 62, but sources said that plan was dropped for now.
"You can bet that in November, IBM will be back saying we didn't get enough people to leave voluntarily," one source said. "They will have to sweeten the offer or lay off people."
